## B. ADR-by-ADR digest

All 15 are **Accepted**. Format `NNNN-short-slug.md`; statuses are Proposed / Accepted / Superseded. Decider is **Yash** on every one.

**0001 — Rent infrastructure, own the application layer** (2026-09-05)
A provider runs Postgres, object storage and CDN; we hand-write every schema, migration, query and endpoint. **No vendor-generated application code.**
*Constraint for extenders:* schema and migrations must stay **provider-agnostic — plain SQL, no proprietary extensions on the critical path** so the exit stays cheap. Rejected: own VPS + Postgres from day 1 (40–60h before the first feature). Revisit when infra cost is material or a requirement (data residency, unsupported extension, custom tuning) managed hosting can't serve.

**0002 — Clients talk to our API, never to the database** (2026-09-05)
All application reads/writes go through an HTTP API we write; clients never hold a DB connection and **never know table or column names**. Exactly three rented pieces of "genuine infrastructure": the OAuth flow, object storage + CDN, and the websocket transport.
*Constraint:* RLS stays on as defence in depth only. The listed rules that **cannot be expressed as RLS** and therefore force server code: queue ranking score, exclusion of already-seen profiles, **3-rejects-then-suppress-90-days**, chat rate limits, first-message contact-detail stripping. Rejected: direct-to-DB BaaS with RLS-only; own-everything-including-auth/uploads/websockets (30–40h against a 60–80h budget). The API contract itself is now an expensive-to-change artefact and "must be versioned and documented deliberately."

**0003 — The API is its own deployable, inside one monorepo** (2026-09-08)
One repo, two independently building/deploying artefacts: `apps/web` and `apps/api`. **Separate deployable, not separate repository.**
*Constraint:* Next.js route handlers are permitted **only** for OAuth callback, image proxying, webhooks — **no business logic**. Four reasons given: makes 0002 enforceable (a network boundary can't be reached past by accident); the runtime model fits (**background jobs: auto-suspend on report threshold, ghost-profile decay at 30/60 days, analytics aggregation**, plus a persistent connection pool); deploy decoupling from un-force-updatable mobile apps; parallelisation across 4 part-timers. Costs: ~4h setup (CORS, token propagation, two local processes), **1–5ms extra SSR hop in-region**. Rejected: API inside Next route handlers; separate repositories.

**0004 — `apps/api` is TypeScript on Node, Fastify + Zod** (2026-09-10)
TypeScript/Node, **Fastify** for HTTP, **Zod** for runtime validation; the **OpenAPI document generated from those schemas is the single source of truth for all clients**.
*Constraints:* runtime validation at every boundary is "a non-negotiable review item"; **CPU-heavy work must not block the event loop — the ranking computation belongs in SQL**; OpenAPI must be generated and committed from day one. Rejected: Kotlin+Ktor (its DTO-sharing advantage is "recoverable later through OpenAPI codegen"; the ramp month is not), Java+Spring (3–4× code per endpoint), Hono (edge portability moot; TS-only RPC typing Kotlin can't consume and which "risks crowding out a real OpenAPI spec"), Express (maintenance mode), Go/Python. **Notable hook: "A Python ML service can be called from this API later if v2 ranking needs one."**

**0005 — Supabase + Firebase + Cloudflare R2** (2026-09-10)
Postgres + Realtime on Supabase Pro ($25/mo); Google sign-in on Firebase Auth; object storage + CDN on Cloudflare R2. **~$50–80/month total at launch.**
*Five non-negotiable rules created:* (1) **our own `users.id` is the PK everywhere; Firebase UID is a plain `auth_provider_id` column only the login path reads**; (2) **never proxy image bytes through the API** — API issues a short-lived presigned upload URL, client uploads directly to R2 and reports the key; (3) **verification selfies in a separate non-public bucket** with short retention, reachable only via short-lived signed URLs after an authorization check; (4) **Realtime is `broadcast` only**; (5) phone OTP, when it lands, goes behind our own endpoints so the SMS provider is swappable.
*Storage model at 20k users:* 45 GB stored (32 GB profile photos = 20k × 4 × ~400KB; 6 GB listing photos = ~2k listings × 8 × ~400KB; 4 GB selfies = 20k × ~200KB), **~700 GB/month egress**, **~14 GB egressed per 1 GB stored**. R2 worth ~$600/mo by 200k users. Wasabi rejected on fair-use policy; B2 rejected on vendor count. Firebase has **no official KMP SDK** — KMP uses `expect`/`actual` over native Firebase SDKs. Lock-in table: Postgres ~none, storage low, realtime low, **identity medium — "only because of Rule 1."**

**0006 — Drizzle as the database layer** (2026-09-10)
Drizzle in **`apps/api` only**; the TypeScript schema is the **single source of truth for the entire database** (not a subset/client view); migrations generated as plain committed `.sql`.
*Constraints:* "`apps/api` owns the schema; **nothing else may import it**"; every schema change ships as a committed `.sql` migration applied in CI; complex analytical queries are written as **raw SQL through Drizzle**, not forced through the query builder. Adoption evidence mid-2026: Prisma 55.3M/30d, Drizzle 48.1M/30d but weekly trend 2.9M→5.1M vs Prisma 3.8M→4.3M; Drizzle overtook Prisma on weekly in Q4 2025, **gained company backing March 2026**. Net **~15–25 hours saved**. Rejected: Prisma (untyped `$queryRaw` exactly where the hardest logic lives), Kysely, raw `pg`.

**0007 — Hybrid rendering, Bearer tokens, instant revocation** (2026-09-10)
Rendering splits **by whether a page needs SEO**: landing / listing browse / listing detail are **server-rendered by Next calling `apps/api` server-to-server, no identity**; stack, liked, chat, settings are **client-rendered with `Authorization: Bearer <Firebase ID token>`**. Bearer is the single auth mechanism on web, Android and iOS — **no session cookies**. `users.tokens_valid_after timestamptz not null default now()` **ships in the first migration**.
*Mechanics:* ID token is a **JWT signed RS256 by Google, ~1 hour lifetime, not configurable**; refresh token is opaque, long-lived, **our API never sees it**. Verification is local against Google's cached public keys — no DB lookup, no Firebase call. Revocation check: `if (decoded.iat * 1000 < user.tokens_valid_after.getTime()) throw unauthorized()`. Explicitly cheaper than Firebase's `verifyIdToken(token, checkRevoked: true)`, which makes a network call per request.
*Constraints:* CORS must be configured on `apps/api` for the web origin; the ID token is XSS-reachable — mitigations are **strict CSP**, Firebase SDK **in-memory** token storage, 1h expiry, instant revocation; the API needs **unauthenticated read endpoints** for listings and landing content. Rejected: everything client-side (forfeits organic search); everything server-side with cookies (web-only ⇒ two auth paths forever). Revisit: a cookie layer can be added **in addition to** Bearer, not replacing it.

**0008 — `apps/web` stack** (2026-09-10)
Next.js 16 App Router, React 19, Tailwind v4, TanStack Query (authed app only). **Existing pages from `femmeflats-design` are ported in, not rebuilt from `create-next-app`.**
*Rationale is correctness, not caching:* without a cancellation guard a late response overwrites fresh data — and **"in a swipe stack `id` changes every second or two," so the race is the main interaction, not an edge case**. ~30–40 fetching components, ~400 lines saved, break-even ~5th endpoint. Gives **prefetching the next N cards** and **optimistic accept/reject with rollback**. *Cost:* query-key design and invalidation strategy ("budget a few hours"). Rejected: plain fetch+useState, SWR (weaker mutations/optimistic updates). Noted as the one **genuinely reversible but asymmetric** decision.

**0009 — Hosting and region** (2026-09-11)
Supabase `ap-south-1`, `apps/api` on Fly.io `bom`, `apps/web` on Vercel pinned to `bom1`.
*Key claim:* the dominating latency is **API→database, not user→API**. Split regions cost ~55ms/query ⇒ **~275ms wasted on a 5-query endpoint**. **Postgres region is sticky; compute follows it.** Only Fly.io has an Indian region among candidates; Render has none, Railway none confirmed.
*The deciding argument:* **serverless functions have no shared memory between requests** — nothing can be buffered, batched, throttled or cached across requests. Three collisions: analytics ingestion (**~65k sessions/mo at 5k WAU, ~150–200 events/session, ~10–13M events/mo, ~50–80 flushes/session ⇒ ~4.2M HTTP requests/mo for analytics alone**; a long-running process buffers ~500-row batches over one persistent connection); **rate limiting (~10 new conversations per user per day — an in-process counter vs an external round trip per message send)**; auto-suspend on report threshold.
*Workload split table:* listings grid ~500k/mo CDN-cacheable → serverless; profile detail ~300k → serverless; swipe queue ~325k, personalised → either; analytics firehose ~4.2M → long-running; rate limits → long-running; background jobs → long-running.
*Vendor data:* Fly $11.2M revenue (2024), ~60 employees, 37,000 customers, **$25M Series D Aug 2026**; Vercel $340M ARR (Feb 2026), ~1,011 employees, **Series F Sept 2025 at $9.3B**. Fly's own messaging: agent-native customers ≈ two-thirds of revenue among its largest, growing ~12× YoY — flagged as real risk, offset because **the deployed artefact is a Docker container** ("the safer vendor carries the riskier coupling").
*Consequences:* **single machine initially — "if it goes down we are down until it restarts"**; two machines later is a one-line config change; Vercel function region must be **explicitly** pinned to `bom1` or SSR silently reintroduces the 55ms problem; Supabase project must be created in `ap-south-1` at the start.
Rejected: Vercel `bom1` as a separate API project (would need **Supavisor, Upstash, QStash** plus a Fastify adapter to reassemble what one process gives free); Railway/Render in Singapore (~50–70ms user latency permanently).

**0010 — pnpm workspaces + Turborepo** (2026-09-11)
pnpm for dependencies (chosen for **strictness** — a package may import only what it declares), Turborepo for tasks.
*Target layout:* `apps/web`, `apps/api`, `packages/contract` (OpenAPI spec + generated types), `packages/config` (shared tsconfig, eslint), `docs/decisions/`. Turborepo over Nx because **Vercel auto-detects it and gives remote caching with zero configuration**, and it is one config file during a month already absorbing Fastify, Zod, Drizzle, TanStack Query, Fly.io and Docker. Nx's real advantage is `affected` (project graph from actual imports), which matters "at twenty packages with a fifteen-minute CI run," not four. Migration later = delete `turbo.json`, `nx init`, ~half a day. Terminology note: Nx deprecated package-based vs integrated in favour of **inferred tasks ("Project Crystal")**. Revisit at ~15 packages or when CI wall-clock becomes a complaint.

**0011 — Design system and the Figma → code token pipeline** (2026-09-14)
femmeflats DS = customised Untitled UI; **Figma is the single source of truth, one-way**. Seven sub-decisions: (1) tokens edited only in Figma — gap path is `DS-GAP` → designer adds it → re-export, **no code → Figma direction**; (2) build input is **`figma-variables.json`, not `tokens.dtcg.json`** because DTCG's `$value` carries only the default mode with the rest in `$extensions["com.figma"].modes`, and the lossless file keeps `valuesByMode` **aliases by id**; (3) `theme.css` generated wholesale, with a **required verification pass that collects every `var(--…)` referenced by Untitled UI React's component source and hard-fails the build if the generated file doesn't define one**; (4) aliases preserved as `var()` references, never flattened — generator rules: literal for primitives, `var(--target)` for `VARIABLE_ALIAS`, **fail the build on `unresolvedAliases`**, cross-collection aliases resolve in the target collection's `defaultModeId`, **name collisions resolve by id never by name** (a stated bridge limitation); (5) **plain `@theme`, never `@theme inline`** — with inline, the value is baked in and `.dark-mode` reassignment has no effect; **dark mode reassigns the semantic token, never the primitive**; (6) **light-first**, dark as a class, so "system" appearance means reading `prefers-color-scheme` in JS and applying `.dark-mode` on the root element ourselves; (7) generated files are **committed** and CI re-runs the generator and **fails if output differs** — so Vercel and Fly builds need no Figma access.
*BLOCKED:* the **naming transform** cannot be written. `token-map.md` proposes `--color-bg-primary` → utility `bg-primary`, but stock Tailwind v4 would generate `bg-bg-primary`. Unblocked by `npx untitledui@latest tailwind` then reading the real `theme.css` — **"its names win."**
*Outstanding:* Brand ramp is still Untitled UI blue, fonts still Inter. When Brand moves to a **rose/red hue, brand and `error` must stay clearly distinguishable** — Block, Report and destructive confirmations cannot read as primary actions. Also: primitives must be emitted into `@theme` or `var()` refs dangle, which is why `check-tokens.mjs` must keep enforcing semantic-token usage.

**0012 — Analytics events live in our own Postgres** (2026-09-14)
All events go to a **separate, append-only Postgres instance we own** — a second Supabase project. No third-party analytics vendor. Monthly partitions, **BRIN index on timestamp**, **buffered batched writes from `apps/api`**, **schema versioned as Zod in `packages/contract` with `event_version` on every row**, rollup tables built by a background job.
*Event lifecycle (per card):* **impression, true view, dwell, deep view, decision** — buffered client-side and flushed **on decision, on an interval, and on `visibilitychange`**. ~65k sessions/mo, ~150–200 events/session, **~10–13M events/mo, ~5 writes/sec average**. Cost ~$25/mo vs ~$390 for PostHog.
*Two consumers named:* humans wanting funnels/retention/activation dashboards, and **"a future ranking model wanting every raw `card_decision` as training signal."**
*Constraints:* separate **instance**, not a separate table, for IOPS/connection isolation; **partition creation must be automated or inserts fail at a month boundary**; we build our own dashboards (deferrable — events accumulate regardless); **retention and deletion policy is now our problem under India's DPDP Act** — account deletion must purge or pseudonymise event history, raw events need a defined retention window, "designed with the schema, not bolted on." Rejected: PostHog (cost + "shipping a sensitive behavioural stream plus our future training corpus into a vendor's system"), own-Postgres+PostHog-on-a-subset, ClickHouse/Tinybird (right at ~10× this volume). Revisit past ~500M rows.

**0013 — CI gate and testing baseline** (2026-09-14)
Every PR runs: **typecheck (whole monorepo, strict) · lint (shared `packages/config`) · `turbo build` · unit tests · API integration tests (Vitest against a disposable real Postgres) · generated-file check (regenerate tokens, fail on diff) · `check-tokens.mjs` · `gitleaks`**. Unit tests are **a coding-time habit**, written in the same pass as the code.
*Two hard constraints:* **CI must finish in ~5 minutes** ("past that, people stop waiting for it and start merging on hope"), and every test is an hour not spent on features out of ~200.
*The four rule areas the integration tests concentrate on:* verification gates participation; `tokens_valid_after` revocation; chat rate limits; queue seen-exclusion and reject suppression. Real Postgres not mocks, because "the queue rules are largely SQL." **Test data setup for the queue rules should be a shared fixture from the start.**
*Deferred:* **Playwright E2E** on signup → verification → swipe → first message (15–20h + maintenance). Rejected: typecheck/lint/build only; full pyramid from day one (40+h).

**0014 — Error tracking and observability** (2026-09-14)
**Instrument with the Sentry SDK in both apps; point the DSN at self-hosted GlitchTip on Fly (~$5/mo).** "Where errors go is a DSN, not a vendor commitment." Mobile in month 4 uses **Firebase Crashlytics** (free). Free-tier uptime monitor on the single Fly machine.
*Why not Vercel logs:* two structural gaps — it sees only `apps/web` (the API on Fly is invisible), and it logs only what runs on Vercel's servers, so **browser errors from the client-rendered authed app never appear at all**, "and that is most user-facing breakage." Also no grouping, alerting, source-map symbolication, release correlation; short retention.
*Why GlitchTip over Sentry free:* the free tier's binding limit is **1 user, not the 5,000-error cap**, and a shared login conflicts with `docs/security/credentials.md`.
*Planned migration:* to **Crashlytics for web at GA** (announced Google I/O 2026, currently **private preview**, built on Google Cloud's Observability Suite). ⚠️ **That migration is NOT the one-variable switch** — Crashlytics is the Firebase JS SDK, a different integration. **Mitigation built from day one: a thin `reportError(err, context)` module (plus breadcrumb and user-context helpers) in `packages/config` or a small shared package; application code calls only that.**
*Constraints:* **PII scrubbing via `beforeSend` is mandatory** — no message bodies, no phone numbers, no precise locations, `Authorization` redacted. ⚠️ **Error tracking runs on the infrastructure it monitors** — if Fly has a problem GlitchTip may be down exactly when needed; accepted knowingly. GlitchTip needs its own Postgres (the analytics instance is the suggested host — "verify GlitchTip's exact dependencies at setup"). Mild admitted tension with ADR 0001's rent-don't-run posture.

**0015 — UUIDv7 primary keys, minted by the client where possible** (2026-09-15)
Every table: `id uuid primary key` holding a **UUIDv7, with no database default**. Declared as:
```ts
id: uuid('id').primaryKey().$defaultFn(() => uuidv7()),
created_at: timestamp('created_at', { withTimezone: true }).notNull().defaultNow(),
```
**Generation priority: client if it can → API if it didn't → never the database.**
*Why not `bigint`:* (1) **enumerability** — `/users/1024` implies 1023 and 1025 exist, "on a women-only safety product that turns any id-taking endpoint into a walkable list of every user"; (2) insert locality is recoverable — v7's **48-bit millisecond timestamp in the high bits** gives "v4's opacity, `bigint`'s locality"; (3) **client-minted ids** make a retried POST naturally idempotent via **`ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING`**, avoiding temp-id reconciliation and a separate idempotency-key column when KMP apps with offline chat ship in month 4.
*Why no DB default:* **Supabase hosted runs Postgres 17; native `uuidv7()` arrived in Postgres 18** — but even after upgrading, a `DEFAULT uuidv7()` means the id exists only after INSERT commits, so offline-first would be dead on arrival.
*Client-minted tables:* `messages`, `swipes`, `reports`, `blocks`. *API-minted:* `users`, `profiles`, `listings`. Same column definition everywhere — **the only difference is whether the endpoint's Zod schema accepts an `id` field at all**.
*Three guards:* spoofed timestamp → **Zod validates the embedded timestamp is within ±5 min of the server clock**; sorting by id → **never sort by the uuid, `created_at` (server clock) is the only chronology the application trusts** ("the timestamp inside a UUIDv7 is an optimisation for Postgres, not data"); id squatting → irrelevant.
*Cost:* +8 bytes per row/FK/index entry; ~160 KB on `users` at 20k; **~1 GB extra index on a 144M-row events table**. Rejected: `bigint` PK + separate opaque `public_id`; API always mints. Revisit at ~500M rows in a single table — **`analytics_events` can switch to `bigint` in isolation, "because nothing ever holds a foreign key to a log line."**

---

## C. Architecture shape

### Package graph
```
femmeflats/
├── apps/
│   ├── web/          Next 16 · Tailwind v4        → Vercel bom1
│   └── api/          Fastify · Drizzle · Zod      → Fly.io bom (Docker)
├── packages/
│   ├── contract/     OpenAPI spec + generated types + versioned analytics Zod schemas
│   └── config/       shared tsconfig, eslint (+ the reportError wrapper, per ADR 0014)
└── docs/decisions/
```
- `packages/contract` holds the **generated, committed OpenAPI document** (ADR 0004) and the **versioned analytics event schemas with `event_version`** (ADR 0012). It is what all clients — web now, KMP Android/iOS in month 4 — generate from.
- `packages/config` holds shared tsconfig and eslint (ADR 0010) and is the nominated home for the `reportError(err, context)` wrapper (ADR 0014).
- **`apps/api` owns the Drizzle schema; nothing else may import it** (ADR 0006). `apps/web` has **no database dependency whatsoever**.
- pnpm enforces that a package may import only what it declares — no reliance on hoisting (ADR 0010).

### Request topology
Clients (web browser + future KMP Android/iOS) hold a Firebase ID token and hit `apps/api` over HTTPS using the generated OpenAPI contract. `apps/api` fans out to Supabase Postgres + Realtime, Cloudflare R2, and Firebase (JWT verification only — actually verified locally against cached Google keys). Next.js SSR pages call `apps/api` **server-to-server** for public data.

### Auth transport
`Authorization: Bearer <Firebase ID token>` — **identical on web, Android and iOS. No session cookies, ever.** ID token = RS256 JWT, ~1h fixed TTL, sent on every request. Refresh token stays on device; **our API never sees it**. Verification = local signature check against Google's cached public keys, plus the local `tokens_valid_after` comparison on the already-loaded user row. Setting `tokens_valid_after = now()` kills every session on every device instantly — the single mechanism behind suspend, ban, log-out-everywhere, compromise response, and the auto-suspend-on-report-threshold requirement.

### Rendering model
Split **by SEO need**: landing / listing browse / listing detail are Next-server-rendered and CDN-cached (no identity, public data — so the API needs unauthenticated read endpoints); stack / liked / chat / settings are browser-client-rendered with Bearer tokens and TanStack Query.

### API boundary rules (the standing rules, verbatim in README and tech-base)
1. Our own `users.id` is the primary key everywhere; the Firebase UID is a plain `auth_provider_id` column. (0005)
2. Every byte entering the API from outside is parsed by a Zod schema before any other code touches it. (0004)
3. The OpenAPI document is generated and committed from day one — the contract all clients generate from. (0004)
4. Image bytes never pass through the API; clients upload directly to R2 via presigned URLs. (0005)
5. Verification selfies live in a separate, non-public bucket. (0005)
6. Realtime is `broadcast` only — no client subscribes to a table. (0005)
7. No business logic in Next.js. Route handlers are for OAuth callbacks, image proxying and webhooks only. (0003)
8. Every primary key is a UUIDv7 with no database default. Never sort by the id — `created_at` (server clock) is the only chronology. (0015)

### Database access rules
Only `apps/api` talks to Postgres, through Drizzle, with a persistent long-lived connection pool (the thing serverless couldn't give). Schema in TypeScript is the sole source of truth for the whole database; migrations are generated plain `.sql`, committed, applied in CI. Analytical/ranking queries are raw SQL through Drizzle with typed results. RLS is on underneath as defence in depth. Two separate Postgres instances: transactional and analytics.

### Hosting / region
`ap-south-1` (Supabase, Mumbai) · `bom` (Fly, Mumbai) · `bom1` (Vercel functions, Mumbai). Region is the sticky choice; compute follows it. One Fly machine initially.

### Primary key strategy
UUIDv7, no DB default, client-minted for `messages` / `swipes` / `reports` / `blocks`, API-minted for `users` / `profiles` / `listings`, ±5 min timestamp validation in Zod, `ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING` for retry idempotence, `created_at` for all ordering.

### Analytics event store
Second Supabase Postgres project, append-only, monthly partitions with automated partition creation, BRIN on timestamp, batched buffered inserts from the long-running API process, rollup tables from a background job, `event_version` per row, schema in `packages/contract`. DPDP-driven retention/deletion is an unbuilt requirement.

### Error tracking
Sentry SDK in both apps → DSN → self-hosted GlitchTip on Fly (its own Postgres, likely co-located with the analytics instance) → planned move to Crashlytics for web at GA, with Sentry Team $26/mo as fallback. All calls go through `reportError(err, context)`. `beforeSend` PII scrubbing mandatory.

### CI gates
typecheck · lint · `turbo build` · unit tests · Vitest API integration tests against disposable Postgres · generated-file check (token generator output must match committed `theme.css`) · `check-tokens.mjs` · `gitleaks`. Five-minute budget. Turborepo remote caching via Vercel. gitleaks also runs as a pre-commit hook.

---

## D. Domain model

Nothing is implemented yet — the README states schema design is **in progress**, deliberately ahead of scaffolding. Confirmed concrete fields are sparse; the named scope is:

### Columns explicitly specified
| Table | Column | Type / definition | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| *every table* | `id` | `uuid primary key`, UUIDv7, **no DB default**, `$defaultFn(() => uuidv7())` | ADR 0015 |
| *every table* | `created_at` | `timestamp('created_at', { withTimezone: true }).notNull().defaultNow()` — the only trusted chronology | ADR 0015 |
| `users` | `id` | our own PK, foreign-keyed by every other table | ADR 0005 Rule 1 |
| `users` | `auth_provider_id` | plain column holding the Firebase UID; **only the login path reads it** | ADR 0005 Rule 1 |
| `users` | `tokens_valid_after` | `timestamptz not null default now()` — **ships in the first migration** | ADR 0007 |
| analytics rows | `event_version` | on every row | ADR 0012 |
| analytics rows | timestamp | BRIN-indexed, monthly partition key | ADR 0012 |

### Entities named (fields not yet specified)
- **`users`** — "our own id as PK, `auth_provider_id` (Firebase UID) as a plain column, `tokens_valid_after` for instant revocation, **verification state**", plus deletion handling.
- **`profiles`** — derived from `users`, API-minted id.
- **attributes** — "profiles and the **rapid-fire attribute model**"; open question recorded as S3: **columns, rows or JSONB**.
- **queue state table** — "per (viewer, target): **unseen → seen → accepted/rejected, reject counts and suppression windows**". Business rules it must support: ranking score (computed in SQL), seen-exclusion, **3-rejects-then-suppress-90-days**.
- **`swipes`** — client-minted ("user can swipe with no signal; queue and flush").
- **`listings`** — flats; API-minted (needs a server-side R2 presign first). **Lister accounts kept separate from user accounts.**
- **lister accounts** — separate entity from `users`.
- **chat**: **threads, messages, message requests, blocks, reports**. `messages`, `reports`, `blocks` are client-minted. Example endpoint shape in tech-base: `POST /threads/88/messages` with body `{ "id": "019abc4f-…", "body": "when can I visit?" }`.
- **`analytics_events`** (named in ADR 0015's revisit clause) — projected **144M rows**; event types per card lifecycle: **impression, true view, dwell, deep view, decision** (`card_decision` named as the ranking-model training signal).

### Schema design order (a dependency chain, not a preference)
1. Identity — `users` ← every other table FKs to this
2. Profile — `profiles`, attributes
3. The queue — who has seen whom, and what they did
4. Listings — flats + lister accounts
5. Chat — threads, messages, requests, blocks, reports
6. Events — analytics, versioned, with a retention policy

### Schema ledger status
| # | Item | Status |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | UUIDv7 primary keys (= ADR 0015) | **Settled** |
| S2 | The `users` table — columns, verification state, revocation, deletion | **Next** |
| S3 | Profiles and the attribute model (columns / rows / JSONB) | Pending |
| S4 | The queue — unseen → seen → accepted/rejected, reject counts, suppression | Pending |
| S5 | Listings — lister accounts kept separate from user accounts | Pending |
| S6 | Chat — threads, messages, message requests, blocks, reports | Pending |
| S7 | Analytics events — `event_version` + DPDP-compliant retention | Pending |

### Business rules the schema must serve (from ADR 0002/0003/0009/0013)
Queue ranking score (must run **inside Postgres**); exclusion of already-seen profiles; 3-rejects-then-suppress-90-days; chat rate limits (~10 new conversations per user per day); first-message contact-detail stripping; verification gates participation (unverified accounts cannot initiate chat); auto-suspend on crossing the report-rate threshold; **ghost-profile decay at 30/60 days**; analytics aggregation.

---

## E. Extension points and gaps

### Explicitly open / deferred / blocked (the tech-base "Still open" table, plus per-ADR)
| Item | Status | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Naming transform for the token generator** | **BLOCKED** on `npx untitledui@latest tailwind` — generator name-mapping rules are "unspecified" until the real `theme.css` is on disk | ADR 0011 |
| **Rebrand** — Brand ramp still Untitled UI blue, fonts still Inter | Outstanding; **brand must stay visually distinguishable from `error`** | ADR 0011 |
| **Event retention & deletion policy (DPDP Act)** | Not designed. Must be designed **with** the schema, not after. Account deletion must purge or pseudonymise event history; raw events need a defined retention window | ADR 0012, S7 |
| **Playwright E2E on critical paths** | Deferred until UI stabilises, "ideally before the first release where a regression would reach real users" | ADR 0013 |
| **`PRD.md` is deprecated (2026-09-14) and must not be cited** | ADRs **0007, 0009 and 0012** were argued from requirement claims it stated — **analytics event volume, chat rate limits, auto-suspend on report threshold, listings as the SEO surface, and the specific event list** — "the *technical* reasoning stands on its own, but those requirement claims should be revalidated against whatever replaces the PRD" | README, ADR 0012 |
| Schema S2–S7 | Pending; S2 (`users`) is next | README |
| Phone OTP | Deferred; must go behind our own `/auth/phone/*` endpoints | ADR 0005 Rule 5 |
| Own analytics dashboards (funnels, D7/D30 retention, activation, accept rate) | Deferred — "events accumulate from day one whether or not anything reads them yet" | ADR 0012 |
| Crashlytics for web migration | Waiting on GA; track Firebase release notes and the `firebase-js-sdk` RFC | ADR 0014 |
| GlitchTip's exact Postgres dependencies | "Verify at setup" | ADR 0014 |
| Automated monthly partition creation | Required or inserts fail at a month boundary — not yet built | ADR 0012 |
| Second Fly machine | "a one-line config change" but not done; single machine = single point of failure | ADR 0009 |
| Monorepo scaffolding itself | Not started. "Then: scaffold the monorepo" — scaffolding `apps/web` with Untitled UI also unblocks ADR 0011 | README |

### What would block an LLM / AI conversational agent layer

**Hard structural gaps — nothing in these docs provides them:**

1. **No queue or message broker of any kind.** Background work is explicitly "a background job" inside the single long-running `apps/api` process (ADR 0003, 0012). ADR 0009 *rejected* the serverless option partly because it would require **Upstash / QStash**, naming them as "more vendors, hours and spend." There is no Redis, no BullMQ, no SQS, no Inngest, no Temporal anywhere in the stack. An agent layer doing multi-second/multi-turn tool loops has nowhere to put durable work, retries, or backpressure.
2. **No vector store, no `pgvector`, no embedding infrastructure.** Never mentioned. Worse, ADR 0001's consequence is a standing constraint: *"keep schema and migrations provider-agnostic — plain SQL, **no proprietary extensions on the critical path**"*. `pgvector` is available on Supabase but adopting it needs an explicit amendment to that rule, and ADR 0009's portability argument (the DB is a `pg_dump` away from any Postgres) weakens with extensions.
3. **No streaming response support.** The entire API boundary is contract-first: **Zod parses every byte in, and a generated OpenAPI document is the single source of truth for all clients** (ADR 0004, standing rules 2 and 3). SSE / chunked token streaming does not fit that request/response contract model, and ADR 0004 explicitly rejected Hono's TS-only RPC typing *because* it "risks crowding out a real OpenAPI spec." Nothing in the docs describes a streaming or long-lived HTTP pattern. Fly's unlimited max duration (vs Vercel's 300s/800s) is the one enabler present.
4. **No websocket infrastructure of our own.** The only realtime transport is **Supabase Realtime, `broadcast` only** (ADR 0005 Rule 6), which is usable for server→client token streaming (the API publishes to a channel, clients subscribe to channels not tables) — but capacity is **500 concurrent connections on Pro, then $10 per additional 1,000**, already projected to be tight at 500–1,500 peak for chat alone. Adding agent-streaming sessions on top of that is a direct cost and capacity hit, and ADR 0005's revisit trigger ("realtime concurrent connections exceed ~5,000") would arrive much sooner.
5. **No LLM vendor, no model, no API key class defined.** `docs/security/credentials.md` has no row for an inference provider key; it would be 🔴 Critical, `apps/api` only. No prompt/versioning story, no eval story, no cost line in the ~$50–80/mo budget (a single line item that would likely exceed the entire current infrastructure bill).
6. **No caching or shared-state tier.** Rate limiting is explicitly **an in-process counter** (ADR 0009). This is a latent scaling trap independent of AI: the moment a second Fly machine is added, in-process counters and the in-memory analytics buffer stop being correct. Any agent layer that needs cross-request state (conversation memory, token budgets, per-user quotas) inherits that same absence.
7. **Event-loop constraint.** ADR 0004: "CPU-heavy work must not block the event loop." Long-lived streaming inference calls are I/O not CPU, so this is survivable, but the guidance pushes heavy work into SQL, which does not apply to inference.
8. **Single Fly machine.** ADR 0009: "if it goes down we are down until it restarts." Agent workloads with long in-flight requests make restarts much more visible.
9. **DPDP / data-sovereignty posture is actively hostile to sending user data to a third-party model.** ADR 0012 rejected PostHog partly on "shipping a sensitive behavioural stream **plus our future training corpus** into a vendor's system," and ADR 0014 mandates `beforeSend` PII scrubbing (no message bodies, no phone numbers, no precise locations). Chat messages and verified-profile data going to an external LLM would need a decision that directly contradicts the stated sovereignty reasoning. The retention/deletion policy that would govern it is the one item explicitly flagged as "genuinely harder" and not yet designed.
10. **Five-minute CI budget and 200-hour launch budget** (ADR 0013) leave no room for eval suites or nondeterministic-output testing; the whole testing philosophy is built around **deterministic** server-side rules.

**Existing hooks that an AI layer can build on (explicitly sanctioned by the docs):**

- **ADR 0004 names the path directly:** *"A Python ML service can be called from this API later if v2 ranking needs one."* That is the sanctioned precedent for a sidecar service — Fly runs Docker containers, so a second Fly app in `bom` is the shape of least resistance, and ADR 0009's whole argument is that containers are portable.
- **ADR 0012 already designates the analytics store as a training corpus** — "a future ranking model wanting every raw `card_decision` as training signal" — append-only, versioned, monthly-partitioned, and deliberately kept in-house for exactly this. It is off the transactional path, so an inference/feature workload there won't compete for swipe-stack IOPS.
- **The `reportError(err, context)` wrapper pattern (ADR 0014)** is the documented precedent for wrapping a swappable vendor SDK behind one internal module. A `packages/`-level LLM client module is the consistent move.
- **Supabase Realtime `broadcast`** is the one available server→client push channel and is already architected so the API writes, applies rules, then publishes — exactly the shape token streaming needs, boundary intact.
- **`packages/contract`** is the established home for versioned Zod schemas (already used for analytics events with `event_version`), so agent tool schemas / message schemas have an obvious home and an obvious versioning convention.
- **UUIDv7 client-minted ids with `ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING`** (ADR 0015) give idempotent retries for free on `messages` — directly reusable for agent turns.
- **`tokens_valid_after`** gives instant, global, one-write revocation for any agent session too.
- The API is a **long-running process with persistent connections and in-memory buffering** — the single property ADR 0009 spent the most words defending, and the property an agent layer most needs.</result>

This is a clickable wireframe prototype for a flat-and-flatmate-finding product. I need a complete inventory of what was designed, because the product is pivoting to an AI-native conversational model and I need to know exactly what UI already exists to keep, cut, or rework.

B. **Navigation map** — how screens connect. Entry points, the primary navigation (tabs? bottom bar?), and every transition triggered by the prototype's JS.

F. **Design language** — colours (exact hex values), fonts, corner radii, spacing, and whether it is light or dark themed. Note the brand name used in the markup.

G. **Anything unfinished** — placeholder text, dead links, TODO comments, screens that exist but aren't reachable.

Be concrete and exhaustive. Quote exact label text and hex values rather than describing them.

lines: +# ADR 0001 — Rent infrastructure, own the application layer
+**Status:** Accepted · **Date:** 2026-09-05 · **Deciders:** Yash
+## Context
+Team of 4 at ~2 hrs/day, targeting launch in ~1 month (~200 person-hours total,
+of which roughly 60–80 are available for backend and infrastructure). Target
+scale for year one is one city, ceiling ~20k registered users.
+Yash wants operational control and wants to learn how systems scale, but also
+wants v1 in front of users quickly.
+## Decision
+For v1 we rent infrastructure: a provider runs Postgres, object storage and the
+CDN. We hand-write the schema, every migration, every query and every API
+endpoint ourselves — no vendor-generated application code.
+## Rationale
+Rework cost is not uniform, and the two layers sit in different buckets:
+- **Cheap to change later:** hosting provider, server size, CDN, region. Moving
+  Postgres between hosts is a dump-and-restore at any scale we will plausibly
+  reach.
+- **Expensive to change later:** data model, API contract, identity/auth model,
+  analytics event schema. These get baked into every client and every stored row.
+So we buy control where it compounds (the application) and rent where it does
+not (the machines). At 20k users in one city there is no scaling problem to
+solve yet — a single modest Postgres instance covers it comfortably.
+## Consequences
+- Effectively zero of the backend hour budget goes to provisioning and babysitting servers.
+- We must keep schema and migrations in version control and provider-agnostic —
+  plain SQL, no proprietary extensions on the critical path — so the exit stays cheap.
+- Self-hosting remains available later as a deliberate exercise against a
+  working system, which is a better teacher than a greenfield setup.
+## Alternatives rejected
+- **Run our own VPS + Postgres from day 1.** Realistically 40–60 person-hours
+  before the first feature ships, plus an ongoing tax, out of a ~200 hour budget.
+  Buys control over a layer that is cheap to reclaim later anyway.
+## Revisit when
+Infrastructure cost becomes material, or a requirement appears that managed
+hosting cannot serve (data residency, an unsupported extension, custom tuning).
+# ADR 0002 — Clients talk to our API, never to the database
+**Status:** Accepted · **Date:** 2026-09-05 · **Deciders:** Yash
+## Context
+Web (responsive) ships first; native Android and iOS follow, with shared
+business logic in Kotlin Multiplatform and native UI in Compose / SwiftUI.
+That means the same rules will eventually be exercised by three clients.
+Managed backends allow clients to query Postgres directly, with Row Level
+Security policies as the only authorization layer. That is the fastest path to
+a v1 and the reason it was considered.
+## Decision
+All application reads and writes go through an HTTP API we write. Client apps
+never hold a database connection and never know table or column names.
+We do rent three pieces of genuine infrastructure from the managed platform:
+the OAuth sign-in flow, object storage plus CDN for images, and the websocket
+transport for chat.
+Row Level Security stays enabled underneath as defence in depth, not as the
+primary authorization mechanism.
+## Rationale
+- Business rules must live in exactly one place. Split across SQL policies and
+  three clients, they drift, and the drift is invisible until a client
+  misbehaves in production.
+- Parts of the spec cannot be expressed as RLS at all: the queue ranking score,
+  exclusion of already-seen profiles, the 3-rejects-then-suppress-90-days rule,
+  chat rate limits, and first-message contact-detail stripping. Server-side code
+  is required regardless — so we should not pretend otherwise and build half a
+  backend by accident.
+- With an API in place, adding a client is adding an HTTP client. Without one,
+  adding a client means reimplementing the rules.
+- Table shapes become an internal detail again, so schema changes stop being
+  breaking changes for shipped mobile apps we cannot force-update.
+## Consequences
+- The API contract itself becomes an expensive-to-change artefact and must be
+  versioned and documented deliberately.
+- Slower to first screen than direct-to-database. Accepted knowingly.
+- Auth token verification must happen in our API, not only at the database edge.
+- The KMP shared module later consumes this same API — no parallel code path,
+  and the web app has already exercised every endpoint in production.
+## Alternatives rejected
+- **Direct-to-database (BaaS), RLS only.** Fastest v1, but couples three clients
+  to the schema and scatters business rules. The expensive-to-change layer would
+  be the one we rented.
+- **Own everything including auth, uploads and websockets.** Maximum portability,
+  but roughly 30–40 extra person-hours against a 60–80 hour budget, spent on
+  problems that are solved and not differentiating.
+## Revisit when
+The rented pieces (OAuth, storage, socket) become a constraint, or costs at
+scale justify bringing one of them in-house. Each is individually replaceable
+because none of them holds business logic.
+# ADR 0003 — The API is its own deployable, inside one monorepo
+**Status:** Accepted · **Date:** 2026-09-08 · **Deciders:** Yash
+## Context
+ADR 0002 established that clients talk to an API we own, never to the database.
+The obvious cheap way to build that API is inside the Next.js app as route
+handlers: one project, one deploy, no CORS, no network hop, free type sharing.
+## Decision
+One repository containing (at least) `apps/web` and `apps/api`. Two artefacts
+that build and deploy independently, sharing tooling and the API contract.
+Separate *deployable*, not separate *repository*.
+Next.js keeps route handlers only for things that belong to the web client
+specifically: the OAuth callback, image proxying, webhooks. No business logic.
+## Rationale
+- **It makes ADR 0002 enforceable rather than aspirational.** If the API lives
+  inside the web app, the database is one import away from every Server
+  Component. Under deadline pressure someone queries it directly because it
+  works, and that rule now exists only in the web client. A network boundary
+  cannot be reached past by accident.
+- **The runtime model fits the workload.** The spec needs background jobs
+  (auto-suspend on report threshold, ghost-profile decay at 30/60 days,
+  analytics aggregation), scheduled work, and a persistent Postgres connection
+  pool. Serverless route handlers make each of these a workaround; a
+  long-running service simply has them.
+- **Deploy coupling.** Otherwise a CSS change redeploys the API that shipped
+  mobile apps — which cannot be force-updated — depend on.
+- **Scaling axes diverge** once mobile ships and most traffic carries no web
+  rendering at all.
+- **Four people at ~2 hrs/day parallelise better** across two deployables with a
+  contract between them than across one codebase.
+## Consequences
+- A few extra hours of setup: CORS, auth token propagation, two local processes
+  (one monorepo task runner command).
+- One extra network hop for server-side rendering — roughly 1–5ms in-region.
+- The monorepo needs a task runner and a shared contract package from day one.
+## Alternatives rejected
+- **API inside Next.js route handlers.** Least setup, fastest first screen, but
+  erodes the client/API boundary and fits the background-job requirements poorly.
+- **Separate repositories.** Hardest boundary, but loses single-clone
+  convenience and splits every contract change across two PRs. A later-stage move.
+## Revisit when
+The web app is the only client and mobile is cancelled, or operational overhead
+of two deployables measurably outweighs the boundary's value.
+# ADR 0004 — apps/api is TypeScript on Node, using Fastify and Zod
+**Status:** Accepted · **Date:** 2026-09-10 · **Deciders:** Yash
+## Context
+Team of four: Yash is Android/Kotlin, at least one member has real server-side
+experience, and the group's stated preferences are JavaScript and Java.
+Roughly 60–80 person-hours available for backend before launch. Native Android
+and iOS follow later, sharing business logic through Kotlin Multiplatform.
+Candidates considered: TypeScript on Node, Kotlin with Ktor, Java with Spring Boot.
+## Decision
+`apps/api` is TypeScript on Node, using **Fastify** as the HTTP framework and
+**Zod** for runtime validation at every external boundary.
+The API contract is expressed as an **OpenAPI document generated from those
+schemas**, and that document is the single source of truth for all clients.
+## Rationale
+**Why TypeScript rather than Kotlin or Java.** The binding constraint is
+person-hours, not throughput — at 20k users in one city, every candidate is
+over-provisioned and only a load test would distinguish them. Two developers
+already prefer JavaScript, AI assistance for TypeScript is materially stronger,
+and a single-language monorepo avoids running Gradle and pnpm side by side.
+Kotlin's real advantage — sharing DTOs directly with the KMP module — is
+recoverable later through OpenAPI codegen. The month spent ramping the team is
+not recoverable. Java was rejected on verbosity and slow feedback loops against
+a two-hours-a-day schedule.
+**Why Fastify rather than Hono or Express.** Fastify is built for exactly the
+long-running Node process ADR 0003 committed to, and ships first-party plugins
+for CORS, rate limiting, JWT, multipart uploads and OpenAPI generation — all of
+which the spec requires. Its schema-first design means the OpenAPI document the
+KMP clients need is a byproduct of routine work rather than a separate chore.
+Hono's headline advantages are edge-runtime portability (moot under ADR 0003)
+and TypeScript-only RPC typing, which Kotlin cannot consume and which risks
+crowding out a real OpenAPI spec. Express is dated and effectively in
+maintenance.
+**Why Zod is mandatory, not optional.** TypeScript types are erased at compile
+time; `as SomeType` is an assertion, not a check. Without runtime parsing at the
+edge, the type safety is theatre. Rule: every byte entering the API from outside
+— request bodies, query params, webhooks, third-party responses — is parsed by a
+schema before any other code touches it.
+## Consequences
+- Runtime validation at every boundary is a non-negotiable review item.
+- CPU-heavy work must not block the event loop; the ranking computation belongs
+  in SQL, which is where it should live anyway.
+- The OpenAPI document must be generated and committed from day one, before any
+  mobile client exists, so it never has to be reconstructed retroactively.
+- Node dependency churn is an accepted ongoing maintenance cost.
+## Alternatives rejected
+- **Kotlin + Ktor** — best long-term fit for the mobile story, rejected on
+  polyglot-monorepo friction, team ramp-up, thinner server ecosystem.
+- **Java + Spring Boot** — most mature, rejected on verbosity and feedback-loop
+  speed against the hour budget.
+- **Go, Python** — nobody on the team knows Go; Python is nobody's preference.
+  A Python ML service can be called from this API later if v2 ranking needs one.
+## Revisit when
+The team composition changes substantially toward JVM, or a workload appears
+that Node genuinely cannot serve. Neither is expected before launch.
+# ADR 0005 — Managed platform split: Supabase + Firebase + Cloudflare R2
+**Status:** Accepted · **Date:** 2026-09-10 · **Deciders:** Yash
+## Context
+ADR 0001 (rent infrastructure) and ADR 0002 (we own the API) mean we need exactly
+four commodity services from providers — and nothing else. No query APIs, no
+generated clients, no vendor-held business logic.
+| # | Need | Used for |
+| 1 | Postgres | All application data |
+| 2 | OAuth / identity | Google Sign-In (phone OTP deferred) |
+| 3 | Object storage + CDN | Profile photos, listing photos, verification selfies |
+| 4 | Websocket transport | Chat delivery |
+## Decision
+| Component | Vendor | Plan |
+| Postgres | **Supabase** | Pro, $25/mo |
+| Realtime transport | **Supabase Realtime** | `broadcast` channels only — never `postgres_changes` |
+| Identity | **Firebase Authentication** | Free to 50k MAU |
+| Object storage + CDN | **Cloudflare R2** | Pay-as-you-go |
+Estimated total at launch scale: **~$50–80/month.**
+## Analysis 1 — Identity
+Compared on consumer social sign-in only. No enterprise SSO, no SMS.
+### Monthly cost by monthly-active users
+| MAU | Firebase / GCIP | Supabase Auth | Clerk | Auth0 | WorkOS AuthKit |
+Published rates used:
+- **Firebase / GCIP** — free to 50k MAU, then graduated: $0.0055/MAU (50k–100k),
+  $0.0046 (100k–1M), $0.0032 (1M–10M). Graduated = each rate applies only to
+  users within that band.
+- **Supabase Auth** — 100k MAU included in Pro, then ~$0.00325/MAU.
+- **Clerk** — ~$0.02/MAU. **Auth0** — ~$0.07/MAU. Both priced for B2B SaaS.
+- **WorkOS AuthKit** — free to 1,000,000 MAU, no time limit, then $2,500 per
+  additional million. Monetised via enterprise SSO connections we would never buy.
+### Why Firebase
+**This is not a cost decision at our horizon.** At 20k–50k MAU every option
+except Clerk and Auth0 is $0. Even at 100k — 5× our stated ceiling — Firebase is
+$275/month, negligible for a business of that size. Optimising here would mean
+optimising a number that does not exist yet.
+The thing that actually differs today is **mobile**:
+- Firebase's Android and iOS SDKs are best in class, and this product will be
+  predominantly a phone app.
+- Google Sign-In integrates with Android Credential Manager / One Tap, which is
+  exactly the zero-typing sign-in the spec calls for.
+- Yash already knows the Firebase mobile SDKs — no ramp-up.
+- Supabase officially supports Firebase as a third-party auth provider, so it
+  will trust Firebase-issued JWTs and RLS still works as defence in depth.
+WorkOS was genuinely tempting on price (free to 1M MAU) but is web- and
+B2B-first: on mobile you wire OAuth/PKCE flows yourself and the native
+experience is materially worse. That is a real cost in month four, paid to avoid
+a bill we will not see for years.
+**Firebase has no official KMP SDK.** This is fine — auth is inherently a
+platform concern, so the KMP module uses `expect`/`actual` over the native
+Firebase SDK on each side. Standard practice, not a workaround.
+## Analysis 2 — Object storage
+### Usage model at 20k registered users
+**Storage:**
+| Item | Calculation | Size |
+| Profile photos | 20k users × 4 × ~400KB | 32 GB |
+| Listing photos | ~2k listings × 8 × ~400KB | 6 GB |
+| Verification selfies | 20k × ~200KB | 4 GB |
+**Egress:**
+| Step | Value |
+| Weekly actives (~25% of registered) | 5,000 |
+| Sessions/month | ~65,000 |
+| Image loads per session (~50 cards × 1.5 photos) | ~75 |
+| Per transformed WebP | ~120 KB |
+| Per session | ~9 MB |
+| Monthly egress incl. listings | **~700 GB** |
+**The decisive ratio: ~14 GB egressed per 1 GB stored** — and it worsens as
+engagement improves. Egress, not storage, is the entire bill.
+### Monthly cost

+| Provider | 20k users
50 GB / 700 GB out | 200k users
500 GB / 7 TB out |
+| Backblaze B2 + Cloudflare | ~$0.30–6 | ~$3–10 |
+| DigitalOcean Spaces | ~$5 | ~$70 |
+| Supabase Storage | ~$15–40 *(plus Pro)* | ~$210–615 |
+| Wasabi | ⚠️ policy violation | ⚠️ policy violation |
+Published rates used: R2 $0.015/GB storage, **$0 egress**, 10GB free tier;
+S3 $0.023/GB + $0.09/GB egress; Supabase 100GB storage and 250GB egress
+included, then $0.0213/GB and $0.03–0.09/GB; B2 $0.006/GB with free egress to
+Cloudflare via Bandwidth Alliance; DO Spaces $5 flat for 250GB + 1TB transfer.
+### Why R2
+- **Zero egress fees**, on a workload that is 93% egress by cost anywhere else.
+  Worth roughly **$600/month by the time we reach 200k users** — more than every
+  other infrastructure line item combined.
+- **S3-compatible API**, so the exit is a bucket copy and an endpoint change.
+- Cloudflare CDN and Image Transformations available natively.
+**⚠️ Wasabi ruled out on policy, not price.** Its "no egress fees" claim carries
+a fair-use expectation that monthly downloads stay *below* stored volume. We are
+at ~14× stored volume and would be in violation from month one. Wasabi is priced
+for backup and archive, not media serving.
+**Backblaze B2 rejected on vendor count.** Marginally cheaper storage, but free
+egress requires Cloudflare in front via the Bandwidth Alliance — a fourth vendor
+to save ~$5/month. R2 already *is* Cloudflare.
+## Analysis 3 — Postgres and Realtime (Supabase)
+Postgres: real Postgres, no proprietary layer on the critical path, `pg_dump`
+is the exit. Supabase is open source and self-hostable, so ADR 0001's
+"self-host later to learn ops" path is a supported migration rather than a
+rewrite.
+**Realtime must be used as `broadcast`, not `postgres_changes`.** The popular
+mode has clients subscribe to changes on a *table*, which would silently
+demolish ADR 0002 — clients would learn our table names and column shapes, and a
+schema change would break shipped mobile apps we cannot force-update. With
+`broadcast`, our API writes the message, applies the rules (rate limit,
+contact-detail stripping, message-request routing), then publishes a payload to
+a channel. Clients subscribe to channels, never to tables. Same feature, same
+cost, boundary intact.
+**Capacity note:** Pro includes 500 concurrent realtime connections, then $10
+per additional 1,000. At 20k registered users, peak concurrent chat could
+plausibly be 500–1,500 — budget an extra $10–20/month.
+## Rules this decision creates
+These are non-negotiable and reviewable:
+1. **Our own `users.id` is the primary key everywhere.** The Firebase UID is
+   stored as a plain `auth_provider_id` column that only the login path reads.
+   Every other table foreign-keys to *our* ID.
+   *Why:* auth is the one piece with real lock-in — you cannot `pg_dump` an OAuth
+   relationship. With this rule, switching providers is a one-column backfill
+   plus a silent Google re-login. Without it, the provider's ID is embedded in
+   every foreign key and the migration is a rewrite.
+2. **Never proxy image bytes through the API.** The API issues a short-lived
+   presigned upload URL; the client uploads directly to R2 and reports the key.
+3. **Verification selfies live in a separate, non-public bucket** with short
+   retention, reachable only via short-lived signed URLs issued after an
+   authorization check. Mixing them with profile photos means one bad bucket
+   policy exposes biometric-grade data.
+4. **Realtime is `broadcast` only.** No client ever subscribes to a table.
+5. **Phone OTP, when it lands, goes behind our own endpoints**
+   (`POST /auth/phone/start`, `/auth/phone/verify`) so the SMS provider is
+   swappable — Firebase SMS in India runs $0.01–0.07 per verification against
+   ~$0.003 for local providers like MSG91.
+## Escape hatches
+| Component | Lock-in | Exit |
+| Postgres | ~None | `pg_dump`, restore, change connection string |
+| Object storage | Low | S3-compatible: copy bucket, change endpoint |
+| Realtime | Low | Transport sits behind our API; swap it, clients unaffected |
+| Identity | Medium | One-column backfill + silent re-login — *only because of Rule 1* |
+## Revisit when
+- Auth cost becomes material (~500k+ MAU) → reassess WorkOS AuthKit.
+- Realtime concurrent connections exceed ~5,000 → compare a self-run websocket
+  tier against Supabase's per-connection pricing.
+- Infrastructure cost overall becomes material → self-host Supabase per ADR 0001.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# sync-session.sh — copy the live Claude Code transcript for this session into the repo.
# Run this before committing, so the repo always carries the latest state of the session.
#
# Usage:  ./tools/sync-session.sh
#
# No network, no Remote Control. Pure file copy.

set -euo pipefail

REPO_ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
SESSION_ID="$(cat "$REPO_ROOT/session/SESSION_ID" | tr -d '[:space:]')"
DEST="$REPO_ROOT/session/transcript/session.jsonl"

# Find the transcript wherever Claude Code put it (the project dir is derived
# from the cwd the session STARTED in, which may not be this repo).
SRC="$(find "$HOME/.claude/projects" -maxdepth 2 -name "${SESSION_ID}.jsonl" -type f 2>/dev/null | head -1)"

if [ -z "$SRC" ]; then
  echo "error: no transcript found for session ${SESSION_ID} under ~/.claude/projects" >&2
  echo "       is this the machine the session ran on?" >&2
  exit 1
fi

mkdir -p "$(dirname "$DEST")"
cp "$SRC" "$DEST"

LINES="$(wc -l < "$DEST" | tr -d '[:space:]')"
BYTES="$(wc -c < "$DEST" | tr -d '[:space:]')"
echo "synced ${LINES} messages (${BYTES} bytes)"
echo "  from ${SRC}"
echo "  to   ${DEST}"
echo
echo "next:  git add session/transcript/session.jsonl && git commit"
EOS

cd ~/Desktop/roomsie && cat > tools/resume-session.sh <<'EOS'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# resume-session.sh — install this repo's bundled Claude Code session onto THIS machine,
# so you can pick the conversation up exactly where it left off.
#
# Usage:  ./tools/resume-session.sh
# Then:   claude --resume 
#
# Works with any Claude subscription or account. Nothing is sent anywhere.
# Remote Control is NOT used and must stay off — this is a local file install only.

set -euo pipefail

REPO_ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
SESSION_ID="$(cat "$REPO_ROOT/session/SESSION_ID" | tr -d '[:space:]')"
SRC="$REPO_ROOT/session/transcript/session.jsonl"

if [ ! -f "$SRC" ]; then
  echo "error: $SRC not found. Is the repo fully cloned?" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# Claude Code stores transcripts per project directory, under a slug made by
# replacing every non-alphanumeric character in the absolute path with a dash.
SLUG="$(printf '%s' "$REPO_ROOT" | sed 's/[^a-zA-Z0-9]/-/g')"
PROJ_DIR="$HOME/.claude/projects/$SLUG"
DEST="$PROJ_DIR/${SESSION_ID}.jsonl"

mkdir -p "$PROJ_DIR"

if [ -f "$DEST" ]; then
  BACKUP="${DEST}.bak.$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)"
  cp "$DEST" "$BACKUP"
  echo "note: existing transcript backed up to $BACKUP"
fi

# Rewrite the original author's absolute paths to this machine's repo path, so
# the resumed session's cwd and file references point somewhere that exists.
python3 - "$SRC" "$DEST" "$REPO_ROOT" <<'PY'
import json, sys

src, dest, repo_root = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]

# Paths as they existed on the machine the session was recorded on.
ORIGIN_REPO = "/Users/yashmangal/Desktop/roomsie"

rewritten = 0
with open(src) as fin, open(dest, "w") as fout:
    for line in fin:
        line = line.strip()
        if not line:
            continue
        try:
            rec = json.loads(line)
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            fout.write(line + "\n")
            continue
        if rec.get("cwd"):
            rec["cwd"] = repo_root
            rewritten += 1
        fout.write(json.dumps(rec) + "\n")

print(f"installed {rewritten} anchored messages")
PY

echo
echo "session installed for this project directory:"
echo "  $DEST"
echo
echo "now run, from $REPO_ROOT:"
echo "  claude --resume $SESSION_ID"
echo
echo "if --resume does not list it, just run 'claude' and pick the session from /resume."
EOS
chmod +x tools/resume-session.sh && bash -n tools/resume-session.sh && echo "syntax ok"

+            fout.write(line + "\n")
+            continue
+        if rec.get("cwd"):
+            rec["cwd"] = repo_root
+            rewritten += 1
+        fout.write(json.dumps(rec) + "\n")
+print(f"installed {rewritten} anchored messages")
+PY
+echo
+echo "session installed for this project directory:"
+echo "  $DEST"
+echo
+echo "now run, from $REPO_ROOT:"
+echo "  claude --resume $SESSION_ID"
+echo
+echo "if --resume does not list it, just run 'claude' and pick the session from /resume."

# The session lives in this repo

This repo carries the full Claude Code conversation in which roomsie is being
planned. Clone the repo, run one script, and you can continue that same
conversation on your own machine, in your own terminal, on whatever Claude
subscription or account you have.

Nothing is streamed and nothing is shared through Anthropic's servers.
**Remote Control is not used and must stay off.** The whole mechanism is a
JSONL file in this repo plus a local copy into your own Claude Code state
directory.

## To continue the session

```bash
git clone git@github.com:magentawood/roomsie.git
cd roomsie
./tools/resume-session.sh
claude --resume $(cat session/SESSION_ID)
```

If `--resume` doesn't list it, start `claude` from the repo root and pick the
session from the `/resume` picker.

## To save your progress back

After you've worked in the session, before you commit:

```bash
./tools/sync-session.sh
git add session/transcript/session.jsonl
git commit -m "session: <what you covered>"
git push
```

## What the scripts do

| Script | Action |
|---|---|
| `tools/resume-session.sh` | Copies `session/transcript/session.jsonl` into `~/.claude/projects/<slug of this repo's path>/<session id>.jsonl`, rewriting the recorded working directory to your clone's path so file references resolve. Backs up any transcript already there. |
| `tools/sync-session.sh` | Finds the live transcript under `~/.claude/projects` by session id and copies it back into the repo. |

The project slug is your clone's absolute path with every non-alphanumeric
character replaced by a dash, which is how Claude Code names project
directories. The script computes it, so you can clone anywhere.

## Caveats, honestly

- **One writer at a time.** The transcript is a single append-only file. If two
  people resume it and both push, the second push overwrites or conflicts on a
  700KB JSONL. Treat it like a lock: one person holds the session, syncs, and
  pushes before the next person picks it up.
- **The transcript is a record of everything said,** including the original
  author's email address and local file paths. That is why this repo is
  private. Scrub before ever making it public.
- **Model differences are fine.** The transcript is a message log, not a
  checkpoint. A different Claude model reads the same history; it just responds
  as itself from there.
- **Skills, MCP servers and plugins do not travel with the transcript.** If the
  original session used them and yours doesn't have them, past tool calls
  remain visible as history but you cannot re-run them.
- **Vendored source material** lives in `docs/source/`, so the session's file
  references still resolve on your machine.
EOS
cat > .gitignore <<'EOS'
.DS_Store
node_modules/
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
*.log
.turbo/
dist/
build/
.next/
session/transcript/*.bak.*
EOS
echo done
